title.en: Interpolate orientation on the rotation manifold

summary: Choose an orientation path for the intended motion; use sign-aligned quaternion interpolation when the objective is a shortest, constant-rate turn.
objective: Choose an orientation interpolation whose intermediate states are valid rotations with predictable motion.
applies_when: A camera, joint or object must move between two orientations.
Poses are blended, retargeted or keyframed.
An orientation is being integrated over time from angular velocity.
intent_signals: the rotation takes a strange path
example_prompts: Move the camera between two orientations smoothly along the shortest turn.
Blend the two poses without the limbs collapsing.
negative_signals: Single-axis rotations, where interpolating the angle is already correct.
not_for: Single-axis rotations, where interpolating the angle is already correct.

principles: Two failure modes are usually merged and should not be. Interpolating the entries of a rotation matrix independently leaves the set of rotations, and the intermediate matrices can shear or scale. Interpolating Euler angles under a fixed convention does stay in the rotation group: every intermediate triple is a proper rotation. What Euler interpolation loses is path and rate control, producing an axis that wanders and a speed that varies, which is a different complaint from producing non-rotations.

For distinct non-antipodal unit-quaternion endpoints, spherical linear interpolation follows their shortest spherical arc at constant rate. Choosing endpoint signs for the shortest orientation path is a separate convention; prescribed turns and rotation splines can serve other motion objectives.

The unit quaternions q and -q represent the same orientation. For a shortest orientation path, align endpoint signs; identical orientations then remain fixed, including nonidentity orientations. A relative 180-degree orientation has endpoint dot product zero and two equally short directions about its relative axis, so declare the tie choice. A full revolution returning to the same orientation needs an explicit axis and angle schedule; endpoint orientations alone do not specify it.
Integrating orientation over time is a separate problem: a first-order step accumulates truncation error and requires renormalisation, so a naive integrator drifts.
implementation: Store orientation as a unit quaternion or a proper rotation matrix. Before quaternion normalization, reject nonfinite components or zero norm as invalid orientation data; use a numerically safe norm evaluation. Convert to Euler angles for display under a stated convention and order when useful.

State the objective before choosing the interpolant. For a shortest, constant-rate turn use spherical interpolation between normalised endpoints with the sign chosen for the shorter arc; for a prescribed axis, a multi-turn motion or continuity across a sequence of keys, use an explicit axis and angle schedule or a rotation spline instead.
When integrating angular velocity, choose the step size deliberately and renormalise, and prefer a higher-order integrator where accuracy matters.
Keep orientation interpolation separate from position interpolation so the two can be timed independently.
For joint chains, interpolate each joint orientation rather than the end-effector pose, unless the task is defined at the end effector.

For shortest orientation interpolation, normalize valid endpoints and negate one endpoint when their dot product is negative. Clamp rounding excursions of the normalized dot product to the inverse-cosine domain. If the aligned endpoints coincide, retain that endpoint orientation; for nearly coincident endpoints use a stable interpolation such as normalized linear interpolation with its approximation stated. Never substitute the identity rotation or normalize the zero midpoint of unaligned antipodes. For a relative 180-degree turn, record the equal-length path choice; prescribed full or multiple revolutions use their explicit axis-angle schedule.
observable_checks: Compare the interpolated matrices with the proper-rotation conditions under a numerical tolerance. Componentwise matrix blending can fail orthogonality; Euler interpolation under a fixed order remains a rotation, so assess its path and rate against the chosen objective rather than expecting shear.

Check the turn against the stated objective: the short arc where that was the goal, and the full prescribed path where a longer or multi-turn motion was intended. An unexpectedly long turn usually means an endpoint sign was not chosen.
Sample the intermediate orientations and confirm they remain valid rotations rather than drifting from unit length.
Play the interpolation at different durations and confirm the path is identical, only slower.

Use a fixed nonidentity endpoint twice and again with its quaternion sign reversed: shortest orientation interpolation must retain that orientation. Check the declared choice for a relative 180-degree turn and handle invalid zero/nonfinite quaternion input without normalization or a fabricated orientation.

creative_affordances: Non-uniform timing, easing and staged turns remain free; the constraint is on the geometric path, not the pacing.
A deliberately wild tumble is fine when it is authored rather than an interpolation artefact.
known_limits: Authored guidance citing one course treatment of quaternion interpolation; it does not compare higher-order orientation splines.
No runtime performance or numerical accuracy has been measured for this record.

claims.statement: Spherical linear interpolation between two distinct unit quaternions parametrises the shortest path connecting them on the unit quaternion sphere and performs the interpolation as a rotation about a fixed axis at constant angular velocity; integrating the quaternion differential equation with a first-order Euler step is inaccurate because of truncation error and requires renormalisation.
claims.scope: Interpolation and integration of rigid-body orientation for distinct, non-antipodal endpoints. It does not describe blending of full poses including position, and it does not claim that the shortest path is the right objective for every motion.
